subject: exogenous categorical variable treated as (K-1) dummy variables

messages.author: 186c1ca2ff63c1ae
messages.subject: exogenous categorical variable treated as (K-1) dummy variables
parts:
Hi all,

Happy new year to all lavaan users!

I started using SEM a few months ago for my work in ecology. In my models I have several exogenous categorical variables. I included them in the equations as (K-1) dummy variables. For example, the variable "growth form" has 3 levels ("woody", "perennial herbaceous", "annual herbaceous"), I therefore treated it as two dummy variables "woody" (1/0) and "perennial herbaceous" (1/0) (the third level "annual herbaceous" being the most frequent in my dataset).

I got the estimates and SE for both "woody" and "perennial herbaceous" dummy variables, but:
- how should I interpret these estimates, relating to the "annual herbaceous" level?
- is it somehow possible to get an overall effect of the original "growth form" variable? (since the basic question I am interested in is whether growth form has an effect on my response variable)

I apologize for such a naive question, but I read a lot about SEM in the last months, and there are still a couple of things that are probably child's play to most of you, but that I could not unravel by myself so far.

Many thanks in advance.

Noëlie

messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: Re: exogenous categorical variable treated as (K-1) dummy variables
parts:
Principles from regression apply here.  (Cohen, Cohen, West and Aiken's (2003) regression text is my favorite.)  As to interpretation, think of your equation as:

Y = intercept + other predictors + b1*woody + b2*peren + error

Since woody and peren are 0-1 variables, their impact is to raise or lower the intercept--you might rewrite the equation as:

Y = intercept + b1*woody + b2*peren + other predictoprs + error

Where the condition is "herbaceous" (your baseline), then woody and peren are both 0 and drop out of the equation.  So then "intercept" is the value of Y for the "herbaceous" condition, when all other predictors are also 0.  (If you are not modeling mean structures, then this is simply the 0 point for Y.)  The b1 and b2 coefficients show the increase in the value of Y, as compared to the "herbaceous" state, when the state is actually "woody" or "peren."  If you do not have interactions, then, b1 and b2 show the increase in Y for each of those states, versus the baseline state, with the other predictors "held constant."
     If there are no interactions, you can estimate the combined effect of this "research factor" by the incremental R2 for Y, comparing a model without these dummy predictors with a model that includes these dummy predictors.
--Ed Rigdon
